intro: The Ninth ends with a string hymn in D♭ major, a semitone below the key in which the symphony began. Mahler lets its long phrases break into smaller and smaller pieces, until even a single viola note can hold the room.

sections.label: A · Violins, then a string hymn
sections.mNote: A forceful violin line opens into divided string parts

sections.label: B · High violins, low contrabassoon
sections.mNote: A held A hangs above the rising bass line

sections.label: A′ · Horn and strings recover the hymn
sections.mNote: The two principal tunes intertwine in D♭ major

sections.label: B′ · Held violins and small wind replies
sections.mNote: Strings thin out around fragments of the two tunes

sections.label: Dev · Strings climb against descending lines
sections.mNote: Woodwinds and brass join another long crescendo

sections.label: A″ · The hymn’s last broad statements
sections.mNote: Strings and winds share the returning melody

sections.label: Coda · High violins and cor anglais
sections.mNote: The last wind replies fall among dwindling string phrases

sections.label: Coda · Adagissimo: strings and long rests
sections.mNote: Muted second violins begin the broken final page

cues.title: The violins speak together
cues.text: Both violin sections begin in unison, with a forceful rising leap and falling phrase. Then the other strings enter quietly, dividing into many lines. The little turn that flickered through the Rondo-Burleske has become part of a hymn.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 9, Universal Edition first-edition full score (Dover reprint, IMSLP353450), p. 164: Sehr langsam und noch zurückhaltend; first and second violins in unison, f lang gezogen; violas, cellos (divided) and basses entering p molto espress. Bettie Jo Basinger’s Utah Symphony guide has the violins present the movement’s primary melody at the outset, marked molto espressivo and absorbing the turn motive of the Rondo-Burleske: https://usuo.org/explore/2016/05/mahler-9-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A hymn tune, and heaven
cues.text: Commentators hear the hymn tune Eventide, “Abide with Me”, in the opening theme. As the theme grows more assertive it also touches a phrase from Urlicht, sung there to “Je lieber möcht’ ich im Himmel sein”: I would rather be in heaven.
cues.evidence: The Mahler Foundation’s page on the movement notes the similarity to the hymn Eventide (Henry Francis Lyte’s “Abide with Me”, 1847): https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-9/symphony-no-9-movement-4-adagio-sehr-langsam-und-noch-zuruckhaltend/ . Bettie Jo Basinger’s Utah Symphony guide places a brief reference to Urlicht in the first theme, before the melody evaporates, and Reinhold Kubik’s Universal Edition note lists Urlicht among the finale’s references: https://usuo.org/explore/2016/05/mahler-9-listening-guide/ ; https://www.universaledition.com/en/Symphony-No.-9-Draft-Score-of-the-First-Three-Movements/P0005537
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A bassoon below the hymn
cues.text: The strings leave a note hanging in the first violin, p subito and morendo. From far below, a solo bassoon marked pp langsam climbs slowly towards it. This small, bare passage will keep returning between the hymn’s much fuller statements.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 9, UE first-edition full score (Dover reprint, IMSLP353450), p. 164: first violin p subito, morendo; first bassoon 1. Solo, pp langsam. Basinger’s Utah Symphony guide has an isolated bassoon remain as the melody evaporates, anticipating the second section, and its ascending idea resurface later: https://usuo.org/explore/2016/05/mahler-9-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A middle section becomes an elegy
cues.text: The movement’s hymn incorporates a direct quotation from the middle section of the Rondo-Burleske. Here it becomes an elegy, a fervent prayer that fits inside the hymn’s falling phrases.
cues.evidence: The Mahler Foundation’s page on the movement says the finale incorporates a direct quote from the Rondo-Burleske’s middle section, which here becomes an elegy: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-9/symphony-no-9-movement-4-adagio-sehr-langsam-und-noch-zuruckhaltend/ . Bettie Jo Basinger hears the Rondo-Burleske’s turn motive absorbed in the theme and a later allusion to its second episode: https://usuo.org/explore/2016/05/mahler-9-listening-guide/

cues.title: An enormous empty space
cues.text: Mahler writes Plötzlich wieder langsam (wie zu Anfang) und etwas zögernd — suddenly slow again, as at the start, and a little hesitant. Contrabassoon and cellos bring back the bassoon’s rising line far below, while the violins, in their highest register, play pp ohne Empfindung — without feeling.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 9, UE first-edition full score (Dover reprint, IMSLP353450), p. 165: Plötzlich wieder langsam (wie zu Anfang) und etwas zögernd; contrabassoon, cellos and basses with the rising figure; first violins pp ohne Empfindung in the high register. Basinger: the contrabassoon and cellos reiterate the B material while the violins articulate a new idea marked ohne Empfindung in an extreme register: https://usuo.org/explore/2016/05/mahler-9-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Mahler’s music in slow motion
cues.text: Reinhold Kubik hears this twenty-minute finale as a review of Mahler’s own music in slow motion: Urlicht, Ablösung im Sommer, the scherzo of the Third, Der Abschied and Oft denk’ ich all echo in it. A circle, he writes, seems to be closing.
cues.evidence: Reinhold Kubik, May 2009, in Universal Edition’s note to the facsimile of the Ninth’s draft: https://www.universaledition.com/en/Mahler-Symphony-No.-9-Original-draft-of-1st-3-Movements.-Facsimile-of-Composers-Manuscript-D-major-for-orchestra/P0005537

cues.title: The hymn returns in pieces
cues.text: The interlude presses forward at Pesante, then a rit. leads to a tempo (Molto adagio) in five flats. The hymn is back, warmed by a horn, the violins and violas told to play stets breitester Strich — always the broadest stroke.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 9, UE first-edition full score (Dover reprint, IMSLP353450), p. 168: Pesante, rit., a tempo (Molto adagio), five flats, stets breitester Strich in the violins and violas, horns. Basinger: a switch to the major mode and the warmth of the horn indicate the return of A, with no interruptions from B: https://usuo.org/explore/2016/05/mahler-9-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Three kinds of death
cues.text: Leonard Bernstein ended his fifth Norton lecture by suggesting that this whole movement prophesies three deaths: Mahler’s own, the death of tonality, and the death of “Faustian” culture in all the arts.
cues.evidence: The Mahler Foundation’s page on the movement reports Bernstein’s speculation at the end of his fifth Norton lecture: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-9/symphony-no-9-movement-4-adagio-sehr-langsam-und-noch-zuruckhaltend/

cues.title: Walter’s melting cloud
cues.text: In his 1936 book on Mahler, Bruno Walter describes this finale as “like the melting of a cloud in the ethereal blue”. Two years later he conducts the performance playing here, with the Vienna Philharmonic.
cues.evidence: Bruno Walter, Gustav Mahler (1936), quoted in Erik Ryding’s Library of Congress essay, p. 3. The essay also documents the recording of 16 January 1938. https://lcweb2.loc.gov/static/programs/national-recording-preservation-board/documents/MahlerSymphonyNo9.pdf

cues.title: Der Abschied in the woodwinds
cues.text: High woodwinds weave intertwining lines that refer to Der Abschied, the farewell that closes Das Lied von der Erde. Beneath them the ascending bassoon idea surfaces again, now without its earlier bleakness.
cues.evidence: Bettie Jo Basinger’s Utah Symphony guide: the recurrence of B begins with intertwining lines in the high woodwinds that reference Der Abschied, with the ascending bassoon idea surfacing beneath, now without its earlier bleak discomfort: https://usuo.org/explore/2016/05/mahler-9-listening-guide/ . Kubik’s note lists Der Abschied among the finale’s references: https://www.universaledition.com/en/Symphony-No.-9-Draft-Score-of-the-First-Three-Movements/P0005537

cues.title: The orchestra leaves the strings
cues.text: The orchestra thins at dim. and morendo. High violins hold a note at ppp above the dwindling winds, an English horn answers with an espr. phrase, and soon only strings remain, marked ersterbend — dying away.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 9, UE first-edition full score (Dover reprint, IMSLP353450), p. 179: dim. and morendo in the woodwinds, first violins ppp sempre on a high note, English horn espr., ersterbend in the strings. Basinger: morendo and ersterbend indications appear, instruments exit and the volume diminishes: https://usuo.org/explore/2016/05/mahler-9-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A page of farewells
cues.text: Adagissimo. Muted second violins begin a small rising phrase, and the remaining strings answer in scraps, with long rests between them. Whole tunes have shrunk to a turn, a falling step, a note held until the next breath.
cues.evidence: Universal Edition score, p. 180: Adagissimo, muted second violins and fragmented string phrases separated by rests.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: “Welt! Lebe wohl!”
cues.text: On the last page of the draft Mahler wrote words over the music: “O Schönheit! Liebe!” — then “Lebt wol! Lebt wol!” and, over the final pianissimo, “Welt! Lebe wohl!” World, farewell. He signs off the draft at Toblach in the first days of September 1909.
cues.evidence: The Mahler Foundation’s page on the movement shows the inscriptions on the last page of the draft, captioned as signed off at Toblach on Thursday, 2 September 1909: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-9/symphony-no-9-movement-4-adagio-sehr-langsam-und-noch-zuruckhaltend/ . Universal Edition’s note to the facsimile dates the draft 1 September 1909 at its end: https://www.universaledition.com/en/Symphony-No.-9-Draft-Score-of-the-First-Three-Movements/P0005537

cues.title: “The day is fine”, one last time
cues.text: On the closing pages the first violins quote the Kindertotenlieder: “Der Tag ist schön auf jenen Höh’n”, the day is fine on yonder heights. The last note is marked ersterbend, dying away.
cues.evidence: The Mahler Foundation’s page on the movement: on the closing pages Mahler quotes the first violins from the Kindertotenlieder, and the last note is marked ersterbend: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-9/symphony-no-9-movement-4-adagio-sehr-langsam-und-noch-zuruckhaltend/ . Bettie Jo Basinger’s Utah Symphony guide has the violins recall the last lines of the fourth Kindertotenlieder song, with morendo and ersterbend marked: https://usuo.org/explore/2016/05/mahler-9-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The last page
cues.text: On the last page the second violins and lower strings play stets mit Dämpfer, always muted, while the first violins play without a mute. Mahler writes Langsam und ppp bis zum Schluss, then Äusserst langsam and pppp, and under the final fermata, ersterbend — dying away.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 9, UE first-edition full score (Dover reprint, IMSLP353450), p. 180: Adagissimo, mit Dämpfer, stets ohne Dämpfer in the first violins, Langsam und ppp bis zum Schluß, Äußerst langsam, pppp, ersterbend under the last fermata. The Mahler Foundation’s page: the last note is marked ersterbend and the last two pages last about six minutes: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-9/symphony-no-9-movement-4-adagio-sehr-langsam-und-noch-zuruckhaltend/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The low instruments take over
transitions.from: A · Violins, then a string hymn
transitions.how: At Plötzlich wieder langsam (wie zu Anfang) und etwas zögernd the music drops to pp. Contrabassoon and cellos take up the rising line the bassoon played before, while the violins, far above, play pp ohne Empfindung — without feeling.
transitions.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 9, UE first-edition full score (Dover reprint, IMSLP353450), p. 165. Basinger: contrabassoon and cellos reiterate the B material; the violins’ new idea is marked ohne Empfindung.

transitions.title: A rit., then the hymn in D♭ major
transitions.to: A′ · Horn and strings recover the hymn
transitions.how: The interlude presses forward at Pesante, then a rit. leads to a tempo (Molto adagio) in five flats. The violins and violas play stets breitester Strich — always the broadest stroke — and a horn adds its warmth.
transitions.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 9, UE first-edition full score (Dover reprint, IMSLP353450), p. 168. Basinger: the major mode and the warmth of the horn indicate the return of A.

transitions.title: A high note above the orchestra
transitions.from: A″ · The hymn’s last broad statements
transitions.to: Coda · High violins and cor anglais
transitions.how: The orchestra withdraws at dim. and morendo. A high violin note sustains at ppp, the woodwinds drop out, an English horn answers with an espr. phrase, and the strings are left alone, marked ersterbend.
transitions.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 9, UE first-edition full score (Dover reprint, IMSLP353450), p. 179. Basinger: morendo and ersterbend indications appear, instruments exit and the volume diminishes.

transitions.title: Muted strings at Adagissimo
transitions.from: Coda · High violins and cor anglais
transitions.to: Coda · Adagissimo: strings and long rests
transitions.how: At Adagissimo the second violins, violas, cellos and basses take their mutes and the strings continue alone, Langsam und ppp bis zum Schluss, their phrases broken by rests.
transitions.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 9, UE first-edition full score (Dover reprint, IMSLP353450), p. 180: Adagissimo, mit Dämpfer in the second violins, violas, cellos and basses, Langsam und ppp bis zum Schluß.

source.title: Mahler, Symphony No. 9, first-edition full score (Universal Edition, 1912; Dover reprint)
source.locator: Movement IV, printed pp. 164–180: violin unison and divided-string hymn; bassoon and contrabassoon interludes; strings alone at Adagissimo on p. 180.

timeline.note: Both violin sections play the opening line together before the other strings enter.
The string hymn opens into divided inner parts beneath the first violins.
A bassoon climbs slowly beneath a held violin D♭.
Contrabassoon and cellos rise beneath the violins’ high A.
Horn and strings combine the two principal tunes in D♭ major.
Woodwind replies pass between harp notes, high violins and low strings.
Winds and brass join the strings’ crossing lines in the long crescendo.
A high violin note remains above the last flute and cor anglais replies.
Muted second violins begin the Adagissimo; the remaining strings answer between long rests.
Second violins, violas and cellos remain after first violins and basses fall silent.

composer.epithet: A conductor who composed in the summers, and wanted each symphony to hold a whole world — the sublime and the street band together.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee, and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. Iglau gave him the sounds that never left his music: bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church. A story he told late in life, to Sigmund Freud, describes running from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was grinding out Ach, du lieber Augustin. Tragedy and the banal, side by side: it is a fair description of half his slow movements.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, studying piano and composition, and sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. His friends were Hugo Wolf and the short-lived Hans Rott, whose symphony sounds so much like Mahler’s own that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony, as he understood it. The cantata Das klagende Lied, completed in 1880, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881. He had already begun the career that would pay for everything else: conducting.
